triples.source_text: Hear this word of the Lord that I take up over you as a lament, house of Israel:

target_units.text: “And you, take up a lament over Israel’s ruler,

triples.relationship: prophetic lament taken up over Israel
triples.rationale: Amos introduces the word taken up over Israel's house as a lament. Ezekiel likewise receives a command to take up a lament over Israel's ruler. Both explicitly frame the prophetic address as lament, with different stated subjects.

triples.source_text: “Virgin Israel has fallen; she will certainly not rise again. She stumbled upon her land; no one will raise her.”

target_units.text: And you will say this word to them: Bring tears down upon your eyes day and night, and let them not cease, because the daughter of My people was utterly crushed, with a very painful wound.
If I go out to the plain, behold, those wounded by the sword; and if I enter the city, behold, the pain of famine! For priest and prophet went to a land they did not know.

triples.relationship: the people pictured as a devastated daughter
triples.rationale: Amos laments fallen Virgin Israel, who has no one to raise her. Jeremiah calls for continuing tears over the crushed daughter of the people and describes sword and famine. Both use a female figure for the people within a lament over national devastation.

triples.source_text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: “From the city out of which a thousand went, a hundred will remain, and from the one out of which a hundred went, ten will remain for Israel’s house.”

target_units.text: And you shall be left few in number, whereas you were as the stars of heaven in multitude, because you did not hearken unto the voice of the Lord your God.

triples.relationship: a greatly reduced remnant of Israel
triples.rationale: Amos predicts that only a hundred will remain from a city where a thousand went out, and ten from a hundred. Deuteronomy likewise warns that the people will be left few in number after their former multitude, linking their reduction to disobedience.

triples.source_text: For thus says the Lord to Israel’s house: “Seek Me and you will live!

target_units.text: Listen with your ears, and follow My ways; listen to Me, and your soul will live amid good things. And I will make with you an everlasting covenant: the holy and sure blessings of David.
Behold, I have given him as a testimony among the nations, a ruler and commander of nations.
Nations that did not know you will call upon you, and peoples that do not know you will flee to you for refuge, because of your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you.
Seek God, and when you find Him, call upon Him; and when He draws near to you,

triples.relationship: seeking and hearing God associated with life
triples.rationale: Amos commands Israel to seek the Lord and live. Isaiah likewise calls for listening to God so that the soul will live and then commands seeking God. Both connect turning toward God with life.

triples.source_text: Do not seek Bethel, do not enter Gilgal, and do not cross over to the Well of the Oath; for Gilgal will certainly be taken captive, and Bethel will be as though it did not exist.”

target_units.text: But you, Israel, do not be ignorant; and Judah, do not enter Gilgal or go up to the house of On, and do not swear by the living Lord.

triples.relationship: shared prohibition on entering Gilgal
triples.rationale: Amos tells the people not to enter Gilgal while rejecting their resort to named sanctuaries. Hosea likewise explicitly tells Judah not to enter Gilgal. The connection rests on the identical place and prohibition, without equating the passages' other place names.

triples.source_text: Seek the Lord and live, so that Joseph’s house does not flare up like fire; it will devour him, and there will be no one to quench it for Israel’s house.

target_units.text: House of David, thus says the Lord: Judge a judgment in the morning, set things straight, and rescue the plundered from the hand of the one wronging him, so that My anger is not kindled like fire and burns with no one to quench it.

triples.relationship: warning of fire with no one to quench it
triples.rationale: Amos calls for seeking the Lord so that Joseph's house does not flare up in an unquenchable fire. Jeremiah likewise calls David's house to just action so that the Lord's anger is not kindled like fire with no one to quench it. The warnings address different houses.

triples.source_text: The Lord makes judgment on high and has placed righteousness upon the earth,

target_units.text: Cloud and gloom surround Him; righteousness and judgment are the establishment of His throne.

triples.relationship: the Lord's rule described through righteousness and judgment
triples.rationale: Amos positively describes the Lord making judgment on high and placing righteousness upon the earth. The psalm likewise names righteousness and judgment as the establishment of His throne. This connection preserves Amos's positive native wording.

triples.source_text: making all things and refashioning them, turning death’s shadow into morning and darkening day into night; He calls for the sea’s water and pours it upon the earth’s surface. The Lord God Almighty is His name,

target_units.text: He builds His ascent into heaven and establishes His promise upon the earth; He calls for the sea’s water and pours it upon the earth’s surface. The Lord God Almighty is His name.

triples.relationship: same-book repeated description of the Lord's power over waters
triples.rationale: Both passages describe the Lord calling for the sea's water and pouring it upon the earth's surface, then name Him the Lord God Almighty. The repeated description connects the book's presentations of His power.

triples.source_text: the One distributing shattering against strength and bringing suffering upon a fortress.

target_units.text: and he will bring low the height of your wall’s refuge, and it will descend to the ground.

triples.relationship: fortified strength brought down
triples.rationale: Amos describes shattering directed against strength and suffering brought upon a fortress. Isaiah likewise announces the height of a wall's refuge being brought low to the ground, sharing the overthrow of fortified strength.

triples.source_text: They hated one who reproved at the gates and abhorred a holy word.

target_units.text: One who disciplines evil people will receive dishonor for himself, and one who reproves an impious person will bring blame on himself.
Do not reprove evil people, so that they may not hate you; reprove a wise person, and he will love you.

triples.relationship: hatred directed at one who reproves wrongdoing
triples.rationale: Amos accuses the people of hating one who reproves at the gates. Proverbs likewise warns that reproving evil people brings dishonor and hatred, describing the hostile reception of correction.

triples.source_text: Therefore, because you struck the poor with fists and accepted choice gifts from them, you built houses of polished stone but certainly will not inhabit them; you planted desirable vineyards but certainly will not drink their wine.

target_units.text: You shall take a wife, and another man shall have her; you shall build a house, and shall not dwell therein; you shall plant a vineyard, and shall not gather its fruit.

triples.relationship: houses and vineyards whose benefits are lost
triples.rationale: Amos warns those who exploit the poor that they will not inhabit their stone houses or drink their vineyards' wine. Deuteronomy's curse likewise describes a house built but not inhabited and a vineyard planted without gathering its fruit.

triples.source_text: For I knew your many impieties, and your sins are strong: trampling the righteous, taking payments and turning aside the poor at the gates.

target_units.text: You shall not pervert the judgment of a poor man in his cause.
You shall keep far away from every unrighteous charge; the innocent and the righteous you shall not kill, neither shall you justify the ungodly for gifts.
And you shall receive no gifts; for gifts blind the eyes of those who see, and corrupt righteous words.

triples.relationship: payments and injustice toward the poor and righteous
triples.rationale: Amos condemns trampling the righteous, taking payments and turning the poor aside at the gates. Exodus forbids perverting a poor person's judgment, killing the innocent or righteous, and accepting gifts that corrupt righteous words.

triples.source_text: Seek the good and not the evil, so that you may live; then the Lord God Almighty will be with you, just as you said,

target_units.text: Let love be without hypocrisy. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good.

triples.relationship: the ethical contrast of good and evil
triples.rationale: Amos commands seeking good rather than evil. Romans likewise commands abhorring evil and clinging to good, presenting the same opposed directions of conduct.

triples.source_text: “We have hated evil things and loved good things.” Restore judgment at the gates, so that the Lord God Almighty may have mercy on Joseph’s remaining ones.

target_units.text: You shall appoint judges and recording officers for yourself in all your cities which the Lord your God gives you, according to your tribes; and they shall judge the people with righteous judgment.
They shall not pervert judgment, neither shall they show partiality, nor take a bribe; for bribes blind the eyes of the wise, and overthrow the words of the righteous.
You shall pursue justly that which is just, that you may live, and enter and inherit the land which the Lord your God gives you.

triples.relationship: restoration of just judgment in the community
triples.rationale: Amos commands restoring judgment at the gates so that the Lord may have mercy on Joseph's remaining ones. Deuteronomy requires appointed judges to judge righteously in the cities, forbids perverted judgment and commands pursuit of justice. The link concerns the required public administration of justice.

triples.source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord God Almighty: “In every square there will be mourning, and in every road it will be said, ‘Alas, alas!’ A farmer will be called to mourning and lamentation and to those skilled in wailing,

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: Call the women who lament, and let them come; send for the skilled women, and let them speak,
and let them take up a dirge over you; let your eyes bring down tears, and let your eyelids flow with water.
For a voice of lament was heard in Zion: How we suffered misery and were greatly ashamed, because we abandoned the land and threw away our dwellings!
Hear God’s word now, women, and let your ears receive His mouth’s words; teach your daughters lament, and each woman her neighbor a dirge.

triples.relationship: summoning skilled mourners for a public lament
triples.rationale: Amos announces mourning in squares and roads and a call involving those skilled in wailing. Jeremiah likewise summons skilled women who lament to take up a dirge and teach lamentation. Both explicitly describe organized public mourning.

triples.source_text: and in every road there will be mourning, because I will pass through your midst,” said the Lord.

target_units.text: I will go through the land of Egypt that night and strike every firstborn in the land of Egypt, both human and animal. Against all the Egyptians’ gods I will execute vengeance. I am the Lord.

triples.relationship: the Lord passing through a people in judgment
triples.rationale: Amos announces mourning because the Lord will pass through the people's midst. Exodus likewise announces His passage through Egypt to strike the firstborn and execute vengeance. The shared passage-and-judgment pattern is applied to different peoples.

triples.source_text: Woe to those desiring the Lord’s day! Why is this Lord’s day for you? It is darkness, not light,

target_units.text: Blow a trumpet in Zion! Proclaim on My holy mountain, and let all who inhabit the land be thrown into turmoil, because the Lord’s day is present; it is near,

a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist. Like dawn a numerous and strong people will be poured over the mountains. Its like has never existed, nor will another follow it through the years, for generations upon generations.

triples.relationship: the Lord's day described as darkness
triples.rationale: Amos warns those who desire the Lord's day that it is darkness rather than light. Joel likewise describes the near Lord's day as darkness and gloom, with turmoil among the land's inhabitants.

triples.source_text: as when someone flees from a lion and a bear falls upon him, then leaps into his house, braces his hands upon the wall, and a snake bites him.

target_units.text: Fear, pit and trap are upon you who dwell on the earth!
Whoever flees the fear will fall into the pit, and whoever climbs from the pit will be caught by the trap, because windows from heaven have opened and the earth’s foundations will be shaken.

triples.relationship: escape from one danger leads into another
triples.rationale: Amos depicts fleeing a lion only to meet a bear, followed by a snake within a house. Isaiah similarly depicts fleeing fear into a pit and climbing from the pit only to be caught by a trap. Both use successive dangers to expose the failure of attempted escape.

triples.source_text: Is not the Lord’s day darkness rather than light, gloom that has no brightness in it?

target_units.text: For the Lord’s great day is near, near and very swift. The sound of the Lord’s day is bitter and harsh; it is appointed mighty.
That day is a day of wrath, a day of affliction and constraint, a day of untimely ruin and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist,

triples.relationship: shared description of the Lord's day as gloom
triples.rationale: Amos asks whether the Lord's day is darkness and gloom without brightness. Zephaniah likewise calls the near Lord's day a day of darkness, gloom, cloud and mist within an announcement of wrath.

triples.source_text: “I have hated and rejected your festivals, and I certainly will not smell a pleasing scent in your festal gatherings,

target_units.text: you will no longer continue. If you bring fine flour, it is futile. Incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons and sabbaths and a great day I cannot endure; fasting and idleness,
and your new moons and your festivals My soul hates. You have become more than enough for Me; I will no longer let your sins go.

triples.relationship: the Lord's rejection of religious festivals
triples.rationale: Amos's divine speaker hates and rejects the people's festivals and festal gatherings. Isaiah likewise declares that His soul hates their festivals and cannot endure their observances. Both challenge the acceptability of outward religious celebrations.

triples.source_text: because even if you bring Me whole burnt offerings and your sacrifices, I will not receive them, and I will not look upon the salvation offering of your display.

target_units.text: Hear, earth! Behold, I am bringing evils upon this people, the fruit of their turning away, because they did not attend to My words and rejected My law.
Why do you bring Me frankincense from Sheba and cinnamon from a distant land? Your whole burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices did not please Me.

triples.relationship: burnt offerings and sacrifices declared unacceptable
triples.rationale: Amos's divine speaker refuses the people's whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. Jeremiah likewise declares burnt offerings unacceptable and sacrifices displeasing after saying that the people rejected God's words and law.

triples.source_text: Remove from Me the sound of your songs; I will not listen to the music of your instruments,

target_units.text: Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

triples.relationship: refusal to hear religious expression
triples.rationale: Amos's divine speaker will not listen to instrumental music in the sequence of rejected festivals and offerings. Isaiah likewise says He will not listen to multiplied supplications because the people's hands are full of blood. One passage names music and the other prayer, while both reject religious expression.

triples.source_text: and judgment shall roll as water, and righteousness as an impassable torrent.

target_units.text: If you had listened to My commands, your peace would have become like a river and your righteousness like a sea wave.

triples.relationship: righteousness described with moving-water imagery
triples.rationale: Amos pictures judgment rolling as water and righteousness as an impassable torrent. Isaiah likewise uses a river for peace and a sea wave for righteousness. The comparison concerns moving-water imagery, without making the passages' surrounding statements identical.

triples.source_text: Did you offer Me slaughtered offerings and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel?

target_units.text: But God turned away and handed them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you offer Me slaughtered victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?

triples.relationship: explicit later quotation of the wilderness-sacrifice question
triples.rationale: Amos asks Israel's house whether it offered sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years. Acts explicitly introduces words from the prophets and repeats that question about sacrifices, forty years and the wilderness.

triples.source_text: You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, their figures that you made for yourselves.

target_units.text: You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, the images you made to worship them. And I will deport you beyond Babylon.’

triples.relationship: explicit later quotation about Moloch and Raiphan
triples.rationale: Amos names Moloch's tent, the star of the god Raiphan and figures made by the people. Acts' prophetic quotation repeats these named objects and the making of their images, adding that the images were made for worship.

triples.source_text: I will deport you beyond Damascus,” says the Lord; God Almighty is His name.

target_units.text: You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, the images you made to worship them. And I will deport you beyond Babylon.’

triples.relationship: later quotation with a different deportation destination
triples.rationale: Amos announces deportation beyond Damascus. Acts' quotation following the same Moloch-and-Raiphan charge announces deportation beyond Babylon. The corresponding deportation statement is retained together with the explicit difference in destination.

triples.source_text: sleeping upon ivory beds and indulging upon your couches, eating young goats from the flocks and milk-fed calves from the herds,

target_units.text: Now there was a certain rich man, and he clothed himself in purple and fine linen, enjoying himself in splendor every day.
And a certain poor man named Lazarus had been laid at his gateway, covered with sores
and longing to be filled with what fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.

triples.relationship: luxurious living beside neglected suffering
triples.rationale: Amos pictures ivory beds, couches and choice meat in a passage that proceeds to indifference toward Joseph's shattering. Luke likewise places a rich man's daily splendor and table beside the afflicted Lazarus longing for its food. The comparison concerns luxury juxtaposed with suffering.

triples.source_text: clapping to the sound of instruments; they reckoned them as lasting, not passing away,

target_units.text: Woe to those rising in the morning and pursuing strong drink, lingering into the evening, for wine will burn them up!
For with lyre and harp, drums and flutes they drink wine, but they do not look at the Lord’s works or consider the works of His hands.

triples.relationship: instrumental music within indulgent drinking
triples.rationale: Amos describes clapping to instruments within the sequence of luxurious dining and wine drinking. Isaiah likewise describes lyre, harp, drums and flutes accompanying wine while condemning lack of attention to the Lord's works. The shared scene is musical indulgence; Amos's statement about things reckoned lasting is not replaced.

triples.source_text: drinking strained wine and anointing yourselves with the finest perfumes, yet suffering nothing over Joseph’s shattering.

target_units.text: The Lord Sabaoth called on that day for weeping, lamentation, shaving and putting on sackcloth,
but they made gladness and exultation, slaughtering calves and sacrificing sheep to eat meat and drink wine, saying, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!”

triples.relationship: wine and pleasure when mourning is called for
triples.rationale: Amos describes wine and fine perfumes without suffering over Joseph's shattering. Isaiah likewise contrasts a divine call to weeping and lamentation with gladness, meat and wine. Both expose pleasure pursued in the face of a need to mourn.

triples.source_text: Therefore now they will be captives from the foremost of the powerful, and horses’ neighing will be removed from Ephraim.

target_units.text: Woe to those rising in the morning and pursuing strong drink, lingering into the evening, for wine will burn them up!
For with lyre and harp, drums and flutes they drink wine, but they do not look at the Lord’s works or consider the works of His hands.
Therefore My people became captive because they did not know the Lord, and there was a multitude of dead through famine and thirst for water.

triples.relationship: indulgence followed by captivity
triples.rationale: Amos announces captivity after the descriptions of luxurious food, music, wine and indifference. Isaiah likewise moves from strong drink, instruments and neglect of the Lord's works to the people's captivity. Both place that outcome after the account of indulgence.

triples.source_text: For the Lord swore by Himself: “I abhor all Jacob’s arrogance and have hated his regions; I will remove the city with all who inhabit it.”

target_units.text: But if you do not carry out these words, I swear by Myself, says the Lord, that this house will become a desolation.

triples.relationship: a divine self-oath announcing desolation
triples.rationale: Amos introduces the Lord swearing by Himself before announcing removal of the city and its inhabitants. Jeremiah likewise records Him swearing by Himself that the royal house will become a desolation if His commands are not carried out.

triples.source_text: If ten men remain in one house, they will die, and those left over will remain.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: “From the city out of which a thousand went, a hundred will remain, and from the one out of which a hundred went, ten will remain for Israel’s house.”

triples.relationship: same-book warnings of shrinking numbers of survivors
triples.rationale: Amos 5 reduces the remaining numbers from cities, including a hundred reduced to ten. Amos 6 describes ten remaining in a house and announces their death while also mentioning those left over remaining. Both develop the book's population-loss warnings without identifying the groups as the same people.

triples.source_text: For look, the Lord commands, and He will strike the great house with fractures and the small house with cracks.

target_units.text: and I will confound and strike the colonnaded house along with the summer house. Ivory houses will perish, and many other houses will be added,” says the Lord.

triples.relationship: same-book destruction reaching different kinds of houses
triples.rationale: Amos 6 announces fractures in the great house and cracks in the small house. Chapter 3 likewise announces striking colonnaded and summer houses and the loss of ivory houses. Both portray judgment reaching different kinds of dwellings, with distinct categories in each passage.

triples.source_text: Will horses pursue upon rocks? Will they remain silent among females? For you turned judgment into anger and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness,

target_units.text: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is Israel’s house, and the man of Judah a beloved new planting. I waited for it to produce judgment, but it produced lawlessness, not righteousness but an outcry.

triples.relationship: judgment and righteousness transformed into harmful results
triples.rationale: Amos accuses the people of turning judgment into anger and righteousness's fruit into bitterness. Isaiah likewise contrasts expected judgment and righteousness with the lawlessness and outcry actually produced. Both describe the failure of expected just conduct through opposed outcomes.

triples.source_text: rejoicing over nothing, saying, “Did we not acquire horns by our own strength?”

target_units.text: Do not say in your heart: My strength and the might of my hand have gotten me this great wealth.
And you shall remember the Lord your God, for He gives you strength to gain wealth, that He may establish His covenant which the Lord sware unto your fathers, as at this day.

triples.relationship: claims of achievement by one's own strength
triples.rationale: Amos quotes people claiming to have acquired horns by their own strength. Deuteronomy warns against saying that one's own strength gained wealth and instead directs remembrance of the Lord who gives strength. Both quote people crediting their own strength, while naming different things acquired.

triples.source_text: “For look, I am raising a nation against you, house of Israel, and they will crush you so that you cannot enter Emath, as far as the Wadi of the West.”

target_units.text: Behold, I am bringing a nation upon you from far away, house of Israel, says the Lord, a nation whose language’s sound you will not understand.
All are strong,

and they will devour your harvest and your bread, and devour your sons and daughters, and devour your sheep and calves, and devour your vineyards and fig orchards and olive groves; and with a sword they will thresh your fortified cities, in which you have trusted.

triples.relationship: the Lord raises a foreign nation against Israel
triples.rationale: Amos announces the Lord raising a nation against Israel to crush it. Jeremiah likewise announces bringing a distant nation against Israel, with strong attackers consuming its produce and attacking fortified cities.

deferred_source_units.source_text: Therefore the understanding person will be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.
deferred_source_units.reason: The understanding person's silence in an evil time was read. A general statement that there is a time for silence did not establish a sufficiently particular counterpart to this reason for silence; no supported match was retained.

deferred_source_units.source_text: Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in Samaria’s mountain! They harvested the firstfruits of nations and entered themselves. House of Israel,
deferred_source_units.reason: The native statement about despising Zion, trusting Samaria's mountain and harvesting the nations' firstfruits was read. A general comparison with confidence in a dwelling did not establish a sufficiently particular passage correspondence; this unit remains pending.

deferred_source_units.source_text: all of you cross over and see; pass from there to Emath Rabba, and go down from there to Geth of foreigners, the strongest of all these kingdoms, to see whether their borders are greater than your borders.
deferred_source_units.reason: The comparison involving Emath Rabba, Geth of foreigners and the kingdoms' borders was read in full. No secure particular passage correspondence was established from the available native place names and comparison; no alternative names were substituted.

deferred_source_units.source_text: You come toward an evil day, drawing near and touching false sabbaths,
deferred_source_units.reason: The actual statement concerns approaching an evil day and touching false sabbaths. Its native wording was retained; the proposed general comparison with rejected observances did not establish the particular connection, and the unit remains pending.

deferred_source_units.source_text: Their relatives will take them and force their way to bring their bones out of the house. He will say to those in charge of the house, “Is there anyone else with you?” He will say, “No more.” Then he will say, “Be silent, so as not to name the Lord’s name.”
deferred_source_units.reason: The account of relatives removing bones and the instruction not to name the Lord's name was read in full. The proposed silence parallel was absent from the supplied target text; no supported match was retained.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: Therefore the understanding person will be silent at that time, because it is an evil time.

target_units.text: a time to tear and a time to sew, a time to be silent and a time to speak,

unresolved_candidates.reason: Ecclesiastes lists times to be silent and to speak but does not specify the understanding person's silence because a time is evil. The general time-for-silence theme was not retained as a sufficiently particular correspondence.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: Woe to those who despise Zion and trust in Samaria’s mountain! They harvested the firstfruits of nations and entered themselves. House of Israel,

target_units.text: Behold, I am against you who dwell in the valley of Sor, the level land, you who say, Who will frighten us? Or who will enter our dwelling?

unresolved_candidates.reason: The target challenges confidence that no one can enter a dwelling. That general confidence theme did not establish a sufficiently particular relation to the source's native Zion, Samaria and nations' firstfruits statement.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: You come toward an evil day, drawing near and touching false sabbaths,

target_units.text: you will no longer continue. If you bring fine flour, it is futile. Incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons and sabbaths and a great day I cannot endure; fasting and idleness,

unresolved_candidates.reason: Isaiah rejects observances including sabbaths, but does not state Amos's approach to an evil day and touching false sabbaths. The particular native correspondence remains uncertain rather than being supplied from a familiar alternative Amos reading.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: Their relatives will take them and force their way to bring their bones out of the house. He will say to those in charge of the house, “Is there anyone else with you?” He will say, “No more.” Then he will say, “Be silent, so as not to name the Lord’s name.”

target_units.text: Revere the Lord God, for the Lord’s day is near. The Lord has prepared His sacrifice and consecrated His invited guests.

unresolved_candidates.reason: The supplied Zephaniah text commands reverence and announces the Lord's day and prepared sacrifice. It does not contain the proposed silence command or the restriction on naming the Lord found in Amos; no unprinted wording was imported.

unresolved_candidates.source_text: Remove from Me the sound of your songs; I will not listen to the music of your instruments,

target_units.text: He will put an end to the multitude of your musicians, and the sound of your psalteries will certainly no longer be heard.

unresolved_candidates.reason: Ezekiel announces the end of musicians and unheard psalteries within the destruction oracle, whereas Amos refuses to listen to instrumental worship. The lexical resemblance was not retained as an additional sufficiently particular relationship.
